That brings us to our next component: crossovers...........
Crossovers are used to filter the frequency ranges that different speakers receive.

For example, crossovers can be used to filter high and mid-range frequencies from going to the sub-woofers; or they can filter out only the high frequencies, allowing the subs to reproduce a fuller range by allowing mid-range frequencies through...
Conversely, crossovers can be used to filter out lower frequencies from the tweeters and mid-range speakers.
Using crossovers to manage and filter the frequencies for the different speakers helps to maximize clarity and minimize distortion.
The features of a crossover that should determine which ones you will purchase are: crossover configuration, filter slopes, and frequencies.
Crossover frequency cut-off - This is what determines the frequency ranges that can be attenuated or eliminated by the crossover.

Crossover Filter Slope - To make it possible to have a subwoofer perform properly anywhere in the system, the sub-woofer crossover must be 18 dB (decibel) / octave or higher. Anything less will allow mid-bass and possible mid-range frequencies to pass to the sub-woofer(s)...
There is no standard configuration for crossovers. However, this configuration is the most common, and illustrates the general features. aphic: Figure 8-8 and Table 8-2 decibel is on tableee

Decibel (dB) - A unit used to express relative difference in power or intensity, usually between two acoustic or electric signals, equal to ten times the common logarithm of the ratio of the two levels.
The amplifier, a vital part of any custom system, is used to increase the power (watts) of the signal from the head unit to the speakers.
